newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries higher at midday, bullish tone cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries higher at midday, bullish tone cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were higher at midday on Friday, demonstrating a bullish inclination to focus on friendly news and shunt aside indications contrary to its liking.
The market got three economic reports today. A 4.6 percent jump in September durable goods orders grabbed headlines near the start of the session.
The leap was twice as big as what the market had expected and it immediately sent prices sharply lower.

A second, more studied glance at the data showed that a majority of the orders gain came from the volatile civilian aircraft component. When that perception sifted through the market, prices erased losses incurred in the immediate aftermath of the report. The orders jump also followed a revised 3.5 percent decline in August.

After digesting the durable goods data, the market gradually reached levels that were nearly unchanged on the day, just ahead of the National Association of Realtors' report on September existing home sales and the University of Michigan's final October consumer sentiment measures.
Sources said the University of Michigan final October consumer sentiment reading was 96.5 versus 94.7 in September. The current conditions index rose to 106.6 versus 102.0 in September.
With those 1000 EDT/1400 GMT releases behind it, the market made its first foray of the session into the plus column and there it remained.
At 1214 EDT/1614 GMT, the 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was up 17/32 to 99-8/32, yielding 6.81 percent, its best level of the day.

"The market's performance underscores once again the bullish sentiment that exists in the Treasury market," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds. "It's not really focusing on bearish news, but only on positive developments."
"Good foreign central bank buying when the market hit its lows after the durable goods orders report" also spurred the market upward, said Flanagan.
"Foreign central bank buying helped to turn us around," he said.
"The market completely ignored the University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey which showed household attitudes remain buoyant with respect to the economy," said Flanagan.
Waldo Best, senior economist at BZW Securities, said the market's performance was "surprisingly positive" given the mixed nature of the economic data.
"There was strong stuff in the data. There was weak stuff in the data," said Best. "The market seems to be focusing on the weaker side."
Best said the market could go a bit higher before some profit-taking kicks in toward the end of the session.
In midday trade, two-year notes were up 3/32 to 99-31/32, yielding 5.89 percent. Five-year notes were up 5/32 to 99-30/32, yielding 6.26 percent.
The 6-1/2 percent ten-year note was up 8/32 to 99-23/32, yielding 6.54 percent.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was up 13/32 to 89-13/32, yielding 6.84 percent.
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 4.99 percent. Six-month rates were down one basis point to 5.11 percent and year bill rates were down two basis points to 5.24 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
